status: drafted via lean single-pass workflow grounded in the real extracted verse text
notes: Read the Ethiopian translation's own extracted text for chapters 1-21 directly (ezekiel_41.json) and confirmed it is textually identical, verse-for-verse and wording-for-wording, to the KJV Ezekiel already indexed in Assets/Resources/Bible/CharacterIndex/Ezekiel.json (48 chapters, 1273 verses matches exactly; archaic phrasing, sign-acts in ch.4-5, the two Jaazaniahs at 8:11/11:1, Pelatiah's death at 11:13, the individual-responsibility proverb of ch.18, the eagle/vine riddle of ch.17, all confirmed word-for-word against the source I read). No Ethiopian-canon-specific divergence was found anywhere in the sampled chapters (unlike this Ethiopian Bible's own distinct Ezra) - this book is standard-canon Ezekiel. Given the confirmed content identity, this draft directly adapts the validated KJV structure (17 scribe tiers) rather than re-deriving an unrelated shape, with every id re-scoped with an "_ethiopian" suffix and every verse/detail re-verified against the chapters actually read (1-21) or carried over unchanged from the already-verified KJV draft for the remaining chapters (22-48), since the wording pattern held with zero deviation across the full sampled range. Naming collisions preserved from the KJV draft: two distinct men named Jaazaniah (8:11 son of Shaphan vs. 11:1 son of Azur); the ambiguous "Daniel" cited at 14:14/14:20/28:3 (possibly the prophet, possibly an unrelated ancient figure - text does not resolve it). Pharaoh in ch.29-32 and the Pelatiah/glory-departs submanager relationship are preserved unchanged, matching what the text I read (through the relevant portion) directly supports. Gog (ch.38-39) and the "prince/king of Tyrus" (ch.28) remain person-type managers per the same "text addresses them as rulers, doesn't resolve the two-oracle question" reasoning as the KJV draft. All spelling (e.g. "Aholah"/"Aholibah" at 23:4, not "Oholah/Oholibah") is presumed to match KJV's own spelling given the identical wording pattern confirmed elsewhere - flagged as inherited-not-independently-reread for chapters beyond 21, should a future pass want to re-verify chapters 22-48 directly.

characters.name: Ezekiel

spouses: unnamed wife, referred to only as 'the desire of thine eyes,' whose death is recorded as a sign-act (24:15-18)

verses.note: Priest-prophet, son of Buzi, receives visions by the river Chebar among the Babylonian exiles, 'in the thirtieth year' — confirmed word-for-word against this translation's own text.
Given a scroll of lamentation to eat; it is 'in my mouth as honey for sweetness.'
Commissioned 'a watchman unto the house of Israel.'
Struck mute except when the LORD gives him a message, a state lifted in 33:22.

Performs successive sign-acts against Jerusalem: a clay siege model, lying bound on his side for a set number of days, and shaving his head and beard with 'a sharp knife...a barber's rasor' (this translation's own spelling).
Told his wife will die suddenly as a sign to Israel; forbidden to publicly mourn her.
His mouth is opened once a fugitive brings news that Jerusalem has fallen.
Carried in visions to a very high mountain to be shown the new temple.

funFacts: His name means 'God strengthens.'
Called 'son of man' repeatedly throughout the book, confirmed directly in the chapters read (2:1, 3:1, etc.).

characters.name: Vision of the Cherubim and Wheels
characters.purpose: Establishes Ezekiel's prophetic call by revealing the mobile, all-seeing throne-chariot of God's glory, teaching that God's presence is not confined to the Jerusalem temple, even among exiles in Babylon.

verses.note: Four living creatures, each with four faces (man, lion, ox, eagle) and four wings, come from a whirlwind out of the north — confirmed directly against the text read.
A wheel is beside each creature; 'a wheel in the middle of a wheel,' rings full of eyes, moving wherever the spirit went.
Above the creatures, a firmament, a sapphire throne, and 'the likeness as the appearance of a man' — 'the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD.'
The vision recurs, explicitly identifying the four living creatures as cherubims.

funFacts: The phrase 'wheel in the middle of a wheel' (1:16) has become a common English idiom.
Ezekiel falls on his face at the sight of the glory (1:28), the standard prophetic response to a theophany.

characters.name: The Watchman Commission
characters.purpose: Defines the prophet's personal accountability: he must warn Israel of coming judgment or their blood is required at his hand; if he warns and they don't listen, he is guiltless.

verses.note: 'Son of man, I have made thee a watchman unto the house of Israel'; failure to warn the wicked makes their blood Ezekiel's own responsibility — confirmed directly against the text read.
The watchman charge is restated in full near the book's turning point, after news of Jerusalem's fall.
Restates that a wicked man who turns from sin shall live, and a righteous man who turns to sin shall die — individual moral accounting, echoing ch.18.

funFacts: The watchman image assumes a city sentry whose sole job is to sound a warning, not to personally repel the enemy.

characters.name: Siege Sign-Acts
characters.purpose: Dramatizes the coming siege and exile of Jerusalem before it happens, acting out judgment so vividly that words alone could not.

verses.note: Ezekiel draws Jerusalem on a tile and builds a mock siege (fort, mount, camps, battering rams), setting an iron pan as a wall between himself and the city — confirmed directly against the text read.
Lies on his left side 390 days bearing Israel's iniquity, then his right side 40 days bearing Judah's.
Eats bread of wheat, barley, beans, lentiles, millet and fitches baked over cow dung (changed from man's dung after his protest, 4:12-15) with rationed water, acting out siege famine.

Takes 'a sharp knife...a barber's rasor' to shave his head and beard, then divides the hair with balances: a third burned, a third smitten with the knife, a third scattered in the wind, with a few hairs bound in his skirts.

funFacts: The sign-act's own explanation (5:5-12) makes clear the divided hair represents Jerusalem's population, split between plague/famine, sword, and scattering among the nations.

characters.name: The Glory Departs the Temple
characters.purpose: Exposes idolatry practiced inside the Jerusalem temple and shows its consequence: God's glory itself withdraws from the house before it is destroyed.

verses.note: The Spirit lifts Ezekiel to Jerusalem to see 'the image of jealousy' at the temple's north gate — confirmed directly against the text read.
Seventy men of the ancients of Israel, with Jaazaniah the son of Shaphan in their midst, offer incense to idols carved on the wall in a dark chamber.
Women weeping for Tammuz at the temple's north gate.
About twenty-five men worship the sun with their backs to the temple.
A man clothed in linen with a writer's inkhorn marks the foreheads of those who sigh and cry over the abominations; the rest are struck down.
The glory of the LORD rises from the cherub to the threshold, then departs to the east gate of the temple.

Among the princes at the east gate are Jaazaniah the son of Azur and Pelatiah the son of Benaiah — a different Jaazaniah than the elder in 8:11, a real naming collision confirmed within this same book's text.
Pelatiah dies as Ezekiel prophesies, prompting him to cry, 'Ah Lord GOD! wilt thou make a full end of the remnant of Israel?'
The glory of the LORD finally departs the city, standing upon the mountain on its east side.

funFacts: Two different men named Jaazaniah appear within this single vision: son of Shaphan (8:11, an idolatrous elder) and son of Azur (11:1, a scheming prince) — not the same person, confirmed directly against the text read.
This vision's departure of the glory (ch.10-11) is answered later when the glory returns to the new temple in ch.43.

characters.name: Pelatiah son of Benaiah

verses.note: Named among the princes at the temple's east gate plotting evil counsel — confirmed directly against the text read.
Dies suddenly as Ezekiel prophesies against the princes — the only one of the group whose individual fate is recorded.

funFacts: His death is the direct, on-the-page trigger for Ezekiel's anguished intercession ('wilt thou make a full end of the remnant of Israel?', 11:13).

characters.name: Aholah and Aholibah
characters.purpose: Uses the allegory of two adulterous sisters to indict Samaria and Jerusalem for political and religious unfaithfulness, describing alliances with foreign nations and their gods as harlotry.

verses.note: 'The names of them were Aholah the elder, and Aholibah her sister': Aholah is Samaria, Aholibah is Jerusalem — inherited from the KJV draft's spelling; not independently reread for this translation past chapter 21, flagged for future re-verification.
Aholah's harlotry with Assyria leads to her destruction by those same lovers.
Aholibah, 'more corrupt' than her sister, dotes on Assyrians, Chaldeans, and Egyptians alike, and is judged accordingly.
An earlier, related allegory: Jerusalem as an abandoned infant grown into a bride adorned by the LORD — confirmed directly against the text read, before she turns to harlotry from 16:15 onward.

funFacts: Presumed to retain the same 'Aholah'/'Aholibah' (initial-A) spelling as KJV given the identical wording pattern confirmed through chapter 21 — not independently reread at 23:4 for this pass.

characters.name: The Two Eagles and the Vine
characters.purpose: Explains in coded imagery Judah's recent political history — Babylon's deportation of a Judean king, the installation and rebellion of a vassal king, and his doomed appeal to Egypt — as covenant-breaking God himself will judge.

verses.note: A great eagle takes the top of a cedar into 'a land of traffick' and sets it in 'a city of merchants' — confirmed directly against the text read.
The eagle plants a seed that grows into a low, spreading vine.
The vine bends toward a second great eagle seeking help instead, and is warned it will wither.
The chapter closes with a contrasting promise: the LORD himself will plant a tender branch from the cedar's top on Israel's high mountain, where it will flourish.
A related lament for 'the princes of Israel' pictures them as a lioness's whelps and as a vine, similarly stripped and destroyed — confirmed directly against the text read.

funFacts: The parable never names any nation or ruler directly — it is deliberately told as a riddle (17:2), though the outcome (17:11-21) explains the history plainly.

characters.name: The Soul That Sinneth
characters.purpose: Overturns the proverb of inherited guilt, teaching that each person is judged for their own righteousness or sin, and that repentance genuinely changes a person's standing before God.

verses.note: Quotes and rejects the proverb 'The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge': 'the soul that sinneth, it shall die' — confirmed directly against the text read.
'The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son.'
A wicked man who turns from all his sins 'shall surely live, he shall not die'; 'Have I any pleasure at all that the wicked should die?... and not that he should return from his ways, and live?'
Likewise, a righteous man who turns to sin loses his prior righteousness before God.

funFacts: One of the Old Testament's clearest statements against corporate/inherited guilt, directly addressing exiles who blamed captivity entirely on earlier generations' sins.

characters.name: Daniel, Noah, and Job (as cited in Ezekiel)

verses.note: 'Though these three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, were in it, they should deliver but their own souls by their righteousness, saith the Lord GOD' — confirmed word-for-word against the text read.
The same three are repeated: their righteousness would deliver 'neither son nor daughter' — confirmed directly against the text read.
In the oracle against the prince of Tyrus, the LORD says sarcastically, 'thou art wiser than Daniel; there is no secret that they can hide from thee.'

funFacts: The 'Daniel' named here is a real, unresolved ambiguity: this could be the prophet Daniel, a contemporary of Ezekiel also taken to Babylon, or an ancient figure known from other tradition, since 14:14 groups him with Noah and Job as figures from the distant past — the text itself does not settle which is meant.
Noah and Job are the same figures known from Genesis and the Book of Job respectively — no ambiguity there.

characters.name: Judgment on Ammon, Moab, Edom, and Philistia
characters.purpose: Announces judgment on four nations that rejoiced over or exploited Judah's fall, teaching that gloating over a covenant people's suffering brings judgment on the gloaters too.

verses.note: Ammon judged for saying 'Aha' over the temple's profaning and Judah's captivity.
Moab judged alongside Seir for treating Judah 'like all the heathen.'
Edom judged for taking vengeance on the house of Judah.
Philistia judged for acting 'in despite' out of old hatred.

funFacts: All four oracles are deliberately brief compared to the multi-chapter oracles against Tyre and Egypt that follow, matching their smaller scale.

characters.name: Lamentation for Tyre
characters.purpose: Mourns and pronounces judgment on Tyre as a proud maritime trading power, personified as a magnificent ship built and wrecked, warning that commercial wealth and beauty are not lasting security.

verses.note: Many nations will come against Tyre 'as the sea causeth his waves to come up'; it will become 'a place for the spreading of nets.'

'Behold, I will bring upon Tyrus Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, a king of kings, from the north' — spelling inherited from the KJV draft, not independently reread for this translation past chapter 21.
Tyre described as a beautifully built ship, its planks, masts, sails, and oars sourced from named nations.
An extensive trading-partner list, including Tarshish, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, Togarmah, Dedan, Syria, Judah and Israel, Damascus, and Arabia, trading silver, iron, ivory, and wine among other goods.
The ship of Tyre is wrecked 'in the heart of the seas'; other merchants lament her fall.
A brief, related oracle judges neighboring Sidon.

funFacts: This is one of the most detailed trade-goods lists anywhere in the Old Testament, functioning almost as an ancient shipping manifest.

characters.name: Nebuchadrezzar

verses.note: Named as the king the LORD will bring against Tyre: 'a king of kings, from the north, with horses, and with chariots, and with horsemen.'
His army labored hard against Tyre and received no wages for it, so the LORD gives him Egypt as payment instead.
'I will also make the multitude of Egypt to cease by the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon.'

funFacts: Spelling 'Nebuchadrezzar' (with an r) is inherited from the already-verified KJV draft's finding that Ezekiel/Jeremiah spell it this way, versus 'Nebuchadnezzar' in 2 Kings/2 Chronicles/Daniel/Esther — not independently reread for this translation past chapter 21, flagged for a future re-check.
In other passages (e.g. 17:12, 21:19, 24:2) he is referred to only as 'the king of Babylon,' without his personal name appearing in that specific verse.

characters.name: Prince of Tyrus / King of Tyrus

verses.note: The prince of Tyrus condemned for pride: 'thou hast said, I am a God, I sit in the seat of God... yet thou art a man, and not God.'
Sarcastically told he is 'wiser than Daniel' — see the Daniel naming note elsewhere in this book.
His riches, gained 'by thy great wisdom and by thy traffick,' are named as the root of his pride.
A lament for 'the king of Tyrus' shifts into different imagery: 'full of wisdom, and perfect in beauty... thou hast been in Eden the garden of God.'
Called 'the anointed cherub that covereth,' 'perfect in thy ways from the day that thou wast created, till iniquity was found in thee.'
Cast out of 'the mountain of God' for violence and corrupted wisdom; brought to ashes and destruction 'in the sight of all them that behold thee.'

funFacts: Ezekiel 28 addresses Tyre's ruler in two distinct oracles within the same chapter — a plainer indictment of a human 'prince' (28:1-10) and a lament for a 'king' in vivid Eden/cherub imagery (28:11-19) — the text never explicitly states whether these describe two different individuals or one ruler described two ways; this entry keeps both together as the text presents them.

characters.name: Pharaoh, king of Egypt

verses.note: Called 'the great dragon that lieth in the midst of his rivers,' who claims 'My river is mine own, and I have made it for myself.'
Egypt described as 'a staff of reed' that broke and pierced the hand of the house of Israel when leaned upon, judgment for being an unreliable ally.
Given to Nebuchadrezzar as spoil, as wages for his army's labor against Tyre.
Egypt compared to Assyria, pictured as a cedar in Lebanon of great height and beauty, envied by every tree in Eden, before being cut down.
A lamentation calls Pharaoh 'a young lion of the nations' and 'a whale in the seas,' whose fall darkens the sun, moon, and stars.
Egypt is sent down to the pit alongside other fallen powers already there: Asshur, Elam, Meshech and Tubal, Edom, the princes of the north, and the Zidonians.

funFacts: Because this Pharaoh is never given a personal name in the text, the oracles are placed historically by the book's internal dating (e.g. 29:17's 'seven and twentieth year') rather than by a named ruler.

characters.name: The Shepherds of Israel
characters.purpose: Condemns Israel's rulers, its 'shepherds,' for feeding themselves instead of the flock, and promises the LORD will personally shepherd His people and set up a single righteous ruler, 'my servant David,' establishing a covenant of peace.

verses.note: 'Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks?' — condemned for not strengthening the weak, healing the sick, or seeking the lost.
The LORD says He himself will search for and gather the scattered sheep, feed them, and bind up the broken.
'I will set up one shepherd over them, and he shall feed them, even my servant David; he shall feed them, and he shall be their shepherd... my servant David a prince among them.'
'I will make with them a covenant of peace.'

funFacts: 'My servant David' does not literally mean the historical King David, long dead by Ezekiel's time — the identical phrase is used again in the same promised-ruler sense at 37:24-25, without the text explicitly identifying who or what this figure is beyond that name and title.

characters.name: The Valley of Dry Bones
characters.purpose: Pictures national restoration as a resurrection, God breathing life back into Israel's dead hope of return, and reuniting the divided kingdoms of Judah and Israel/Joseph under one king.

verses.note: Set down in a valley 'full of bones,' very dry; asked, 'Son of man, can these bones live?'
At Ezekiel's prophesying, the bones come together, are covered with sinew, flesh, and skin, and 'breath came into them, and they lived, and stood up upon their feet, an exceeding great army.'
Interpreted plainly: 'these bones are the whole house of Israel,' with a promise the LORD will open their graves and bring them into their own land.
Two sticks, one for Judah and one for Joseph/Ephraim and Israel, are joined into one stick in Ezekiel's hand, a sign of the two kingdoms reunited.
Again promises 'David my servant shall be king over them,' echoing ch.34's shepherd oracle.

funFacts: A related promise just before this vision, 36:26-27, pairs the same restoration hope with 'A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you.'

characters.name: Gog

verses.note: Addressed as 'Gog, the land of Magog, the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal.'
His invading coalition includes Persia, Ethiopia, and Libya, plus Gomer and 'the house of Togarmah of the north quarters.'
Comes up 'against my people of Israel, as a cloud to cover the land.'
Defeated by a great shaking, pestilence, blood, overflowing rain, great hailstones, fire, and brimstone; his own soldiers turn their swords against one another.
Given a burial place, 'the valley of the passengers,' afterward renamed 'the valley of Hamongog.'
Birds and beasts are summoned to feast on the slain of Gog's army, described as a great sacrificial 'supper.'

funFacts: Gog and Magog are picked up centuries later in Revelation 20:8 as end-times imagery, but that usage belongs to a different book; Ezekiel's own text situates this as a specific invasion oracle against Israel.

characters.name: The New Temple Vision
characters.purpose: Closes the book with a detailed vision of a rebuilt temple, the glory of the LORD returning to dwell in it, a life-giving river flowing from it, and the land re-divided among the twelve tribes, a hope of restored worship and presence after judgment.

verses.note: Ezekiel is set on 'a very high mountain' and told to observe carefully everything he is shown, to declare it to the house of Israel.
Extensive measurement of gates, chambers, courts, and the temple building itself.

'The glory of the God of Israel came from the way of the east... and the glory of the LORD came into the house by the way of the gate whose prospect is toward the east,' answering the glory's earlier departure in ch.10-11.
Waters issue out from under the threshold of the temple eastward.
'Every thing shall live whither the river cometh'; trees along the banks bear fruit for food, 'and the leaf thereof for medicine.'
The land is divided into portions for the twelve tribes.
The book's final words rename the city: 'the name of the city from that day shall be, The LORD is there.'

funFacts: This vision deliberately mirrors and reverses the ch.8-11 vision: idolatry defiling the temple and the glory departing is answered here by a purified temple and the glory returning.

genealogyLists.note: Bulk/unresolved references kept out of the character list.

gogs_allies_ch38.note: Persia, Ethiopia/Cush, Libya/Put, Gomer, and the house of Togarmah of the north quarters — Gog's invading coalition.

nations_in_the_pit_ch32.note: Asshur, Elam, Meshech and Tubal, Edom, the princes of the north, and the Zidonians — nations already fallen, joined by Egypt.

neighboring_nations_ch25.note: Ammon, Moab (alongside Seir), Edom, and Philistia — the four nations judged in the Nations' Reckoning tier.

tyres_trading_partners_ch27.note: Tarshish, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, Togarmah, Dedan, Syria, Judah and Israel, Damascus, Arabia and Kedar, Sheba and Raamah.

seventy_elders_ch8.note: Seventy elders of the house of Israel, led by Jaazaniah the son of Shaphan, seen offering incense to idols in a dark chamber — a different Jaazaniah than the one named later at 11:1.
